0.title: Song of Songs: Love Strong as Death
0.overview:
The Song of Songs is a love poem. It is the voice of a bride and her bridegroom, delighting in each other, longing for each other, losing and finding each other, and at last declaring that love is strong as death (8:6). Its title, The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's (1:1), calls it the finest of all songs, and Scripture records that Solomon's songs numbered more than a thousand (1 Kgs 4:32). There is no other book of the Bible like it.

It is full of gardens, vineyards, spices, springs, gazelles and doves. It speaks frankly about desire and the body, and it is never crude. The ESV prints labels over the speeches (She, He, Others), and its first footnote explains that these are the translators' additions, based on the gender and number of the Hebrew words. God is named only once, in the very flame of the LORD (8:6), yet the whole poem is set within his world and his gift of marriage.

Christians have often been unsure what to do with the Song, and for centuries many read it only as an allegory, with every detail standing for something in the soul or the church. That reading can lose sight of what the book plainly is. The first meaning of the Song is its plain meaning: it celebrates the love of a husband and wife. God made man and woman for each other: they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed (Gen 2:24-25). The Song is that verse set to music. It honours married love, including its physical delight, as a good gift of the Creator: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4).

The Song also guards that gift. Three times the bride charges the young women of Jerusalem that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). The bride is a garden locked (4:12), kept for her husband, and opened to him gladly (4:16). Desire is honoured by being kept for its time and its covenant.

At its heart is mutual belonging: My beloved is mine, and I am his (2:16), then I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (6:3), and finally I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (7:10). And at its climax is the book's great declaration: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it (8:7).

But the Song does not stand alone in the Bible, and the rest of Scripture shows that marriage itself is a picture. The LORD calls himself Israel's husband: I will betroth you to me forever (Hos 2:19), and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa 62:5). Paul quotes Genesis 2 and says, This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). The Bible ends with a wedding: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready (Rev 19:7).

So the Christian reads the Song in two ways at once, without confusing them. It is a song about marriage, to be believed and enjoyed by husbands and wives. And because every true marriage is a small echo of the love of Christ for his church, the Song also stirs the heart toward the Bridegroom whose love is stronger than death, who laid down his life for his bride, and who says of her, in the end, there is no flaw in you (4:7).

This commentary takes the book chapter by chapter, with a little more room for chapters 1 and 8, where the Song begins and reaches its climax. Every quotation of the ESV has been checked against the ESV text, and every note about the Hebrew rests on the ESV's own footnotes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of Songs and the First Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's (v. 1). The bride longs for her beloved: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine (v. 2). His name is like poured-out oil (v. 3). Draw me after you; let us run, and the king brings her into his chambers, while others rejoice with them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The Bible's great love song opens with desire that is honest, joyful and directed to one beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.

The title tells us what kind of book this is and how highly it is to be valued. The Song of Songs is built like "King of kings" or "holy of holies": the finest of songs, the song above all songs. Solomon, Scripture says, wrote many: He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005 (1 Kgs 4:32). Of all of them, this is the one given the title.

And it is a love song. There is no other book in the Bible like it. No law, no history, no prophecy, and God is named only once, near the end, in the very flame of the LORD (8:6). It is a poem of desire and delight between a man and a woman, full of gardens, vineyards, perfume and longing. The ESV prints labels over the speeches (She, He, Others), and its footnote says honestly that these are the translators' additions, based on whether the Hebrew words are masculine or feminine, singular or plural.

How should a Christian read it? First, as what it plainly is: a celebration of love between husband and wife. God made man and woman, and he made them for each other: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed (Gen 2:24-25). The Song is that verse set to music. Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4). A church that is embarrassed by this book has become more prudish than God.

Second, because Scripture itself says that marriage is a picture of something greater, the Song also lifts our eyes. Paul quotes Genesis 2 and adds, This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). Every true marriage is a small echo of the love of Christ for his bride. So the Song is not a code in which every detail stands for a doctrine. It is a love song about marriage that, read in the light of the whole Bible, makes the heart long for the love of which all marriage is a picture.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine; your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine;

The Song begins in the middle of desire. No introduction, no scene-setting: a woman longing to be kissed. And it is the woman who speaks first. In a book from Solomon's world, which often treated women as property, the Bible's love song opens with a woman's voice and a woman's longing, spoken without shame.

Notice the change of person. Let him kiss me, and then your love. She begins speaking about him and ends speaking to him, the way love does when the beloved comes near. And his love is better than wine: sweeter, more gladdening, more intoxicating than the best the table can offer.

your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.

His fragrance fills the room, and so does his name. A person's name in Scripture is his character and reputation. His is like perfumed oil poured out: it spreads, and everyone who comes near it is drawn. She is not the only one who admires him; virgins love you. He is worthy of love, and she knows it.

A believer reading these lines can hardly help thinking of the one whom Psalm 45 describes: You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips (Ps 45:2). The love of Christ is better than wine. And the order of the Song is the order of the gospel: we are drawn to him because his love came first. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers. We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers.

Draw me: she wants him to lead, and she wants to follow eagerly, let us run. Love is not reluctant. And the king does bring her in, into his private rooms, the place of intimacy. He is called the king, and throughout the Song the bridegroom is spoken of in royal terms. To the woman who loves him, her husband is a king.

We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.

Now others join in: We will exult and rejoice in you. Love between a husband and wife is private, and it is also something the community celebrates. Every wedding feast says so. And the chorus agrees with the bride: rightly do they love you. He deserves it.

For the Christian, the prayer Draw me after you; let us run is the prayer of every heart that has tasted the love of Christ. We do not come to him on our own; Jesus said that no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). But when he draws, we run. When did you last run to him, rather than drag your feet?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am very dark, but lovely: the sun has darkened her while her brothers made her work the vineyards, and her own vineyard she has not kept (vv. 5-6). She asks where her beloved pastures his flock (v. 7), and is told to follow the tracks of the flock to the shepherds' tents (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Love sees and delights in the one who feels unseen and unlovely.

verseByVerse.quote: I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.

The bride turns to the women of the city, and her words carry both embarrassment and confidence. I am very dark, but lovely. The tents of Kedar were the black goat-hair tents of desert nomads; the curtains of Solomon were rich royal hangings. She is dark like the one, and lovely like the other.

Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!

She explains. Her skin has been darkened by the sun, because she has been working outdoors. Her brothers were angry with her and sent her to labour in the vineyards. In a court where beauty meant pale, pampered skin, she looks like a field worker, and she feels it. Do not gaze at me. And she has had no time to care for herself: my own vineyard I have not kept.

Many people know that feeling. The mother who has given years to others and feels she has let herself go. The person who has been shamed by family and carries it into every room. She stands before the fashionable women of Jerusalem and wants to hide.

But she also says but lovely, and the rest of the chapter shows why she can say it: her beloved thinks so. Love does not wait for us to become beautiful before it delights in us. The love of Christ is like that. He did not love a church that was already spotless; he loved her so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27). His love makes lovely.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions? If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions?

You whom my soul loves: the phrase will return again and again (3:1-4). Her beloved is pictured as a shepherd, and she wants to know where to find him at midday rest. She does not want to wander among the other shepherds' flocks like a veiled woman looking for company, a figure who might be mistaken for someone of doubtful reputation. She wants him, and only him.

If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.

The answer comes lightly, perhaps teasingly: if you do not know, follow the tracks of the flock. And it calls her most beautiful among women, the very woman who had just asked not to be gazed at.

The picture of the shepherd who makes his flock lie down at noon is familiar from the Psalms: He makes me lie down in green pastures (Ps 23:2). And Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). The soul that loves him wants to know where he is, and the way to find him is still to follow in the tracks of the flock, among his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Beautiful in Each Other's Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He compares her to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots and praises her adornment (vv. 9-11). She speaks of him as a fragrance close to her heart (vv. 12-14). Behold, you are beautiful, my love, he says; Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, she answers, and their meeting place is green, with beams of cedar and rafters of pine (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Married love is a delight each gives the other in words as well as in presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

Now he speaks, and his first words are praise. To modern ears a comparison to a horse may sound odd, but in Solomon's world the horses of Pharaoh's chariots were prized animals, beautifully harnessed and adorned. She stands out like that. She said, Do not gaze at me. He cannot help it.

Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.

He notices details: her cheeks, her neck, her jewellery. Love pays attention. And the ESV notes that the you in verse 11 is feminine singular: the gift of gold and silver is for her. She came feeling like a field hand; she is treated like a queen.

Husbands, notice what the bridegroom does. He speaks his admiration aloud, specifically, and he gives. Many wives have not heard specific words of delight from their husbands in years. The Song teaches men to say them.

verseByVerse.quote: While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.

She answers with fragrance. Nard was a costly perfume from far away. While the king reclined, her perfume filled the room: her love for him is like that, spreading to where he is.

My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.

A small bag of myrrh worn at the breast keeps its scent close all day and night. So is he to her: close to her heart, never out of her awareness. And like a cluster of henna flowers in the oasis of Engedi, a green place of springs in the desert by the Dead Sea, he is refreshment in a dry land.

Twice she says My beloved is to me. Not what he is to others, but what he is to her. That is how love speaks. And it is how faith speaks of Christ: not only that he is lovely, but that he is lovely to me, the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves.

He says it twice. You are beautiful. The woman who did not want to be looked at is told, again, that she is beautiful. Her eyes are like doves: gentle, soft, perhaps quick and bright. Love repeats itself, because the heart that is loved needs to hear it more than once.

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.

And she says it back. The same words, returned: you are beautiful, my beloved. Their love is mutual, each delighting in the other. Then she looks around their meeting place. It seems to be outdoors: the couch is the green grass, the beams and rafters are the branches of cedar and pine overhead. The whole world has become their house.

Here is a picture of marriage as God meant it: two people who look at each other and say, you are beautiful, and mean it, and find that wherever they are together is home. That love has to be tended, and much of the rest of the Song will show how. But it begins here, in delight given and returned.

1.title: The Song of Songs: Let Him Kiss Me
1.overview:
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's (v. 1) is the finest of songs, a love poem between a bride and her bridegroom. The ESV's speaker labels are the translators' additions. The bride longs for her beloved's kisses, declares his love better than wine, and asks him to draw her after him; the king brings her into his chambers, and others rejoice with them (vv. 2-4).

She is self-conscious before the daughters of Jerusalem, dark from working in her brothers' vineyards and without time to care for herself, yet she says she is lovely (vv. 5-6). She asks where her shepherd pastures his flock and is told to follow the flock's tracks (vv. 7-8).

He praises her beauty and promises her ornaments of gold (vv. 9-11). She speaks of him as a sachet of myrrh close to her heart (vv. 12-14). Each tells the other, you are beautiful, and their green meeting place becomes their home (vv. 15-17).
1.theology:
God created marriage and the delight of husband and wife, and the Song celebrates that gift without shame (Gen 2:24-25; Heb 13:4). Desire within marriage is good, mutual and to be spoken (vv. 2, 15-16).

Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:31-32). Read in that light, the Song shows love that comes first and draws the beloved (v. 4; 1 John 4:19), and love that delights in one who feels unlovely and makes her lovely (vv. 5-6, 15; Eph 5:27).
1.examples:
A woman's voice speaking first, and without shame.

The mother who feels she has let herself go.

A sachet of myrrh worn close to the heart all day.

A husband who has not said a specific word of admiration in years.

A couch of green grass under cedar branches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — His Banner over Me Was Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She calls herself a simple wildflower, and he calls her a lily among brambles (vv. 1-2). She delights in his shade and fruit (v. 3). He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love (v. 4). She is faint with love, held in his embrace (vv. 5-6), and charges the daughters of Jerusalem that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Love protects and displays the beloved, and it must be kept for its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys. As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.

Hymns have often sung these words about Christ, but in the Song it is the bride who says them, about herself. And she is not boasting. The ESV notes that the flower meant is probably a bulb, "such as a crocus, asphodel, or narcissus", the ordinary wildflowers that covered the coastal plain of Sharon in spring. She is saying, I am just one flower among thousands in the field.

As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.

He takes her modest words and turns them around. Yes, a lily, but a lily among brambles. To him every other woman is a thorn bush, and she is the one flower. She says, I am ordinary. He says, you are the only one.

That is what love does to a person who thinks little of herself. It does not argue her into self-esteem. It simply sees her differently and says so. And it is how Christ sees his people: not as one more face in the crowd, but as his own, known by name.

verseByVerse.quote: As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men.

She answers with a matching picture. Among the forest trees, which give shade but no food, he is an apple tree: shade and fruit together. Every other man is ordinary timber; he is the one who nourishes.

With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

Two gifts of the apple tree: shade from the heat, and sweet fruit. She rests in his protection and enjoys what he gives. A good husband is both: a shelter his wife can rest under, and a source of delight.

The believer knows this double gift in Christ. His shadow is refuge; his fruit is sweet. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! (Ps 34:8).

verseByVerse.quote: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.

The ESV notes that the banqueting house is in Hebrew "the house of wine": the place of feasting and celebration. He brings her in, and over her flies his banner. A banner marked where an army belonged and whose they were. His banner over her, the flag that says to everyone whose she is, is love.

What a thing for a woman to be able to say about her husband: when he brings me into company, everyone can see that he loves me. He is not ashamed of her; he displays his love.

And the church can say it of Christ. He has brought us to his table, and the banner over us is not our record or our achievements, but his love. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8).

Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.

She is faint, overwhelmed, sick with love, and asks for raisin cakes and apples to revive her. Anyone who has been deeply in love knows the lightheadedness. The Song does not treat that as silly. It is part of the gift.

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!

The picture is of lovers lying together, his left arm cradling her head, his right arm around her. It is tender and intimate, and the Song does not blush at it. This is the embrace of marriage, and God calls it good.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.

And immediately a warning. The ESV notes that I adjure you means "I put you on oath", and that the phrase is used throughout the Song. This charge will be repeated twice more (3:5; 8:4). Having described the delight of love's embrace, the bride turns to the unmarried young women and puts them under oath: do not awaken this before its time.

Sexual love is like a fire. In the hearth of marriage it warms a home; set loose too early, it burns the house down. Do not stir it up by what you watch, what you read, how you touch, where you let your imagination go, before the time God has made for it. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor (1 Thess 4:3-4).

This is not a word only for teenagers. It is a word for the married person tempted to awaken desire for someone who is not his spouse. Love has its time and its place, and guarding it is part of loving well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Arise, My Love, and Come Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the hills, and stands gazing through the lattice (vv. 8-9). Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past (vv. 10-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14), and asks that the little foxes be caught (v. 15). My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The beloved comes and calls; love answers, guards what is precious, and rests in mutual belonging.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.

A new scene. She hears his voice before she sees him, and her heart leaps. He is coming, and nothing slows him down: mountains and hills are nothing to him. Love finds a way.

My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.

Swift and strong like a young stag, he arrives at her house and stands outside, looking in through the window lattice. He wants to see her. He will not force the door; he calls.

That is a lovely picture of how Christ comes to his people. He does not break down doors. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.

His invitation is one of the most beautiful passages in the book. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away. Come out of the house; come with me. And the reason is spring. In Israel the winter is the season of cold rains; now it is over.

The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.

Everything is coming to life: flowers, birdsong, figs, vine blossom. The ESV notes that singing may be rendered "pruning", the season when vines are cut back for growth. Either way, the world is new, and he wants to enjoy it with her. And he ends as he began: Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.

Marriages go through winters: seasons of grief, illness, distance, dullness. This passage is a call to notice when spring comes, and to go out together into it. When did you last say to your husband or wife, come away with me?

And for the believer, there is a greater spring coming. The winter of this fallen world will end, and the one who loves his church will call her to come away with him into a world made new.

verseByVerse.quote: O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.

She is like a dove hiding in a rock crevice, shy, out of reach. Perhaps she is still hesitant to come out. He does not drag her out. He tells her what he wants: let me see your face, let me hear your voice. And he tells her why: your voice is sweet, your face is lovely.

Some people hide from those who love them, afraid to be seen or heard. Love coaxes them out with gentleness and assurance. That is also how the Lord deals with timid hearts. He wants to hear your voice in prayer, not because he needs information, but because he delights in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."

The ESV notes that the animals may be jackals. Either way, small animals got into vineyards in spring and destroyed the tender blossoms before the grapes could form. The love of the couple is like a vineyard in blossom, and it needs protecting.

It is seldom the great disasters that destroy a marriage. It is the little foxes: the unkind word left unapologised for, the screen that takes the evening, the small resentments, the busyness, the neglect. Catch the foxes for us: it is a shared job. Name the little foxes in your own marriage, or friendship, or walk with God, and catch them before they spoil the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies. Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.

Here is the heart of the Song in a single line. My beloved is mine, and I am his. Mutual belonging. Not ownership in the sense of control, but the covenant belonging of marriage, where each gives himself to the other. The ESV notes that he grazes may be rendered "he pastures his flock": he is still the shepherd, among the lilies.

The line will return, reversed, I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (6:3), and again, I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (7:10). Notice the movement: first she speaks of possessing him, then of belonging to him, and finally of resting in his desire for her. Love matures from "he is mine" to "I am his".

That is the movement of faith too. The believer begins by rejoicing that Christ is his. He grows into the deeper joy that he belongs to Christ. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14).

Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.

Until the morning breeze comes and the night shadows go, she asks him to come to her, swift as a gazelle over the mountains. The ESV notes that cleft mountains may be rendered "mountains of Bether". The chapter ends with longing for him to be near through the night.

2.title: My Beloved Is Mine, and I Am His
2.overview:
The bride calls herself a common wildflower, and her beloved calls her a lily among brambles; she calls him an apple tree among forest trees, and delights in his shade and fruit (vv. 1-3). He brings her to the banqueting house, and his banner over her is love; faint with love, she rests in his embrace (vv. 4-6). She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 7).

Her beloved comes leaping over the hills and calls through the lattice, Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for winter is past and spring has come (vv. 8-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14) and asks that the little foxes that spoil the vineyards be caught (v. 15). My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 16-17).
2.theology:
Married love is a protecting, public and delighting love (vv. 3-4), and its physical expression is good (v. 6; Heb 13:4). Desire must not be awakened before its time; sexual purity is God's will (v. 7; 1 Thess 4:3-5).

Love must be guarded against small threats (v. 15). Husband and wife belong to each other in covenant (v. 16; 1 Cor 7:4). Christ's love is a banner over his people (v. 4; Rom 5:8); he comes and calls rather than forces (vv. 8-9; Rev 3:20), and his people belong to him (John 10:14).
2.examples:
A crocus among thousands on the plain.

A banner that tells everyone whose you are.

A fire in the hearth, and a fire loose in the house.

A face at the lattice, and a voice calling come away.

The screen that takes the evening: a little fox.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not.<sup>2</sup>I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.<sup>3</sup>The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"<sup>4</sup>Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.<sup>5</sup>I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.<sup>6</sup>What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?<sup>7</sup>Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel,<sup>8</sup>all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.<sup>9</sup>King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon.<sup>10</sup>He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Sought Him Whom My Soul Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On her bed by night she seeks him whom my soul loves and does not find him (v. 1). She rises and searches the city, and asks the watchmen (vv. 2-3). Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go (v. 4). Again she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until it pleases (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Love that has known the beloved cannot rest in his absence; it seeks until it finds and holds fast.

verseByVerse.quote: On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not. I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not.

The scene is night. She lies in bed and reaches for him, and he is not there. Whether this is a dream, a memory of the days before the wedding, or simply the ache of absence, the feeling is plain: longing. Him whom my soul loves appears four times in these four verses. She cannot say his name without saying how much he means to her.

I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.

She does not lie still and wait for the feeling to pass. She gets up and goes out into the dark city to look for him. That is not proper behaviour for a young woman at night, and she does not care. Love makes people bold.

Believers know nights like this. The sense of God's nearness is gone, and the soul reaches out and finds nothing. Isaiah prayed it: My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you (Isa 26:9). The right response to such a night is not to roll over and wait, but to rise and seek him: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?" Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"

The night watchmen find her, and she does not even explain herself. She simply asks, Have you seen him whom my soul loves? As if everyone must know who she means. The one who loves assumes the whole world knows the beloved.

Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.

And then, just past the watchmen, there he is. I held him, and would not let him go. She brings him home, into the family house, the place of safety and belonging. Having found him after such a night, she will not lose him again.

Scripture has other pictures of holding on. Jacob wrestled through the night and said, I will not let you go unless you bless me (Gen 32:26). Mary Magdalene went looking in the dark for the body of her Lord, took him for the gardener, and when he spoke her name, held on to him, so that he said, Do not cling to me, for he had still to ascend to the Father (John 20:15, 17). The risen Christ is now found by faith, and faith holds him and will not let him go. And beneath that grip is a firmer one: he holds us.

verseByVerse.quote: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.

The refrain of 2:7 returns word for word. After a scene of intense longing, the bride again puts the young women under oath. Longing like this is powerful. It is exactly why it must not be stirred up before its time.

The repetition matters. No book of the Bible celebrates desire more openly than the Song, and it also warns more than once about awakening it too soon. The two go together. Those who treasure love most will guard it most carefully.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense? It is Solomon's litter, guarded by sixty mighty men (vv. 6-8), his carriage made of cedar, silver, gold and purple, inlaid with love (vv. 9-10). Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The wedding day is the king's day of gladness, and all are called out to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?

A new scene, and a grand one. Something is approaching from the wilderness, and from a distance all anyone can see is a cloud of dust or incense smoke rising like pillars, and all anyone can smell is perfume: myrrh, frankincense and costly spices. A procession is coming.

For Israelite ears, a column rising from the wilderness would recall the pillar of cloud that led their fathers through the desert. That may be only an echo. But it lends the moment a sense of glory: something wonderful is on the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel, all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel,

It is the king's litter, which the ESV's note describes as "the couch on which servants carry a king". Around it march sixty warriors, the best of Israel's soldiers. This is a royal wedding procession, bringing the bride, or the king himself, to the wedding.

all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.

The guards are armed against terror by night: bandits on the road, attackers in the dark. The bride travels in safety. The king protects what he loves. A husband who loves his wife makes her safe.

The believer travels under the same kind of guard. You will not fear the terror of the night (Ps 91:5).

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon.

The ESV notes that carriage may be rendered "sedan chair". It was made of cedar from Lebanon, the finest timber of the ancient world, the wood of the temple itself.

He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.

Silver posts, a gold back, a purple seat: royal splendour. And the inside was inlaid with love by the women of the city, perhaps with embroidery or decoration made as a wedding gift. The most beautiful thing about the carriage was not the gold but the love worked into it.

A home can be furnished with silver and gold and still be cold. What makes the inside beautiful is love worked into it, day by day, by the people who live there.

verseByVerse.quote: Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.

The women of Zion are called out to see the king on his wedding day. He wears a crown given by his mother, a wedding crown, and the day is called the day of the gladness of his heart. Of all the days of Solomon's reign, with its wealth and wisdom and temple building, this one is named as the day his heart was glad.

A wedding is meant to be a day of joy for the bridegroom as much as for the bride. Psalm 45 describes a royal wedding in the same spirit, where the bride is led to the king with joy and gladness (Ps 45:14-15).

And Scripture points to another Bridegroom and another wedding. Jesus spoke of the cry at midnight, Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him (Matt 25:6). The only crown this King was given on earth was not from his mother but from soldiers: the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head (John 19:2). Yet even that day had a gladness hidden in it. He went to the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb 12:2), the joy of a Bridegroom winning his bride. One day the daughters of Zion will go out and see him crowned with glory on the day of his wedding, and the gladness of his heart will be complete.

3.title: Him Whom My Soul Loves
3.overview:
By night the bride seeks him whom my soul loves and does not find him. She rises and searches the city, asks the watchmen, and finds him just past them; she holds him and will not let him go until she has brought him to her mother's house (vv. 1-4). Again she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time (v. 5).

A royal procession rises from the wilderness like columns of fragrant smoke: Solomon's litter, guarded by sixty warriors against the terrors of the night (vv. 6-8), his carriage of cedar, silver, gold and purple, its interior inlaid with love (vv. 9-10). The daughters of Zion are called to see King Solomon wearing the crown his mother gave him on his wedding day, the day of the gladness of his heart (v. 11).
3.theology:
True love seeks the beloved in his absence and holds fast when he is found (vv. 1-4); the believer seeks the Lord in seasons when he seems far (Isa 26:9). Desire must still be kept for its time (v. 5).

Marriage is a day of royal joy, and a husband protects and honours his bride (vv. 6-11). The wedding of the king points to Christ the Bridegroom (Matt 25:6), who wore a crown of thorns for the joy set before him (John 19:2; Heb 12:2) and will rejoice over his bride.
3.examples:
Reaching across the bed in the dark and finding no one.

"Have you seen him?", as if everyone must know who.

Sixty guards against terror by night.

A carriage whose finest feature is the love worked into it.

The day of the gladness of his heart.

Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.<sup>2</sup>Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young.<sup>3</sup>Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, you are beautiful, my love (v. 1). He praises her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, cheeks and neck, and her breasts like twin fawns (vv. 1-5). He will go to the mountain of myrrh until the day breathes (v. 6). You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The bridegroom's love sees the whole of his bride, and to him she is without flaw.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil.

This is the wedding night, or near it, and the bridegroom begins by saying what he said in chapter 1, twice over: you are beautiful. Then he takes his time. What follows is a song of praise that moves over his bride from her eyes downward, one feature at a time. Love does not glance. It gazes, and it names what it sees.

Her eyes are doves behind her veil, glimpsed, gentle, bright.

Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.

To our ears, goats are not flattering. But picture the view: a flock of black goats flowing down a far hillside in the evening light, a dark wave rippling over the slope. That is her long dark hair as it moves. The images belong to the shepherd's world of the Song, and they are meant as the highest compliment.

verseByVerse.quote: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young.

Freshly washed sheep are white, and every one is paired with its twin: her teeth are white, even and complete, none missing. In a world without dentists, that was a real beauty.

Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.

Red lips like a scarlet cord; cheeks flushed like a cut pomegranate, glowing behind the veil. Every line is specific. The bridegroom has paid attention.

Husbands can copy him, and the verse gives the method: notice, then say it. Most spouses long to hear specific praise far more often than they do. Generic compliments are easy. Detailed delight takes attention, and attention is a form of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Your neck is like the tower of David, built in rows of stone; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your neck is like the tower of David, built in rows of stone; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors.

Her neck is tall and straight, and adorned with necklaces like the shields hung on a fortress wall. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word behind rows of stone is uncertain. The picture is of dignity and strength. She carries herself like a queen.

Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.

The praise is frank, and it is tender. Fawns are soft, gentle and lovely, and the picture belongs to a husband delighting in his wife's body. Scripture is not embarrassed by that delight within marriage; Proverbs commands it: rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:18).

The same Bible that forbids lust outside marriage celebrates desire within it. The difference is not the body or the desire, which God made. It is the covenant. Inside it, this kind of praise is holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go away to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense. You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go away to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.

He echoes her words from 2:17, Until the day breathes and the shadows flee. Where she had asked him to come to her through the night, he now says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense: fragrant heights, which in the flow of the poem seem to picture his bride herself. He will stay with her through the night.

You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.

The praise ends in a summary. Altogether beautiful. No flaw in you. Of course she had flaws. The woman of chapter 1 knew it well. But this is how a loving husband sees his wife, and says so: not blind to reality, but seeing her through the eyes of love, as a whole, and delighting in the whole.

And here the Song reaches toward something only the gospel can make fully true. Of his church, which is anything but flawless now, Christ intends that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish (Eph 5:27). He has reconciled us in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Col 1:22). What the bridegroom says in love, Christ will one day make literally so: there is no flaw in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — A Garden Locked, a Fountain Sealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride (v. 8). You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; her love is better than wine (vv. 9-11). A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed, full of choice fruits and spices, a well of living water (vv. 12-15). She answers, Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride keeps herself for her husband alone, and gives herself to him freely and gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Depart from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Depart from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.

For the first time he calls her my bride, and he uses the word five times in verses 8-12. He calls her to come away from the high, wild mountains of the north, Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon, places of lions and leopards. The ESV notes that Depart may be rendered "Look". Either way, he calls her from what is remote, dangerous and lonely, to himself.

Marriage calls a person out of the old life into a new one. It is also how the Lord calls his people: out of the dens of lions, to come with him.

verseByVerse.quote: You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace. How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice! Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace.

My sister, my bride. "Sister" here is not a word of blood but of closeness: she is family to him, bound to him for life, not merely desired. And she has captivated his heart. One glance, one jewel on her necklace, and he is undone. The king is overpowered by his bride.

How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!

In chapter 1 she said your love is better than wine (1:2). Now he says the same to her. The love that began with her longing is fully returned.

Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.

Honey and milk: the words of the promised land, a land flowing with milk and honey. His bride is a promised land to him, sweetness and plenty. Her kisses are sweet, and so are her words.

verseByVerse.quote: A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.

Three pictures of one truth. A garden with a locked gate, a private spring, a sealed fountain: she has kept herself for him. Her body and her love were not open to anyone who passed by. They were reserved for her husband.

Proverbs uses the same imagery for faithfulness in marriage: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well, Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:15, 18). The locked garden is chastity before marriage and faithfulness within it.

In a culture where the gate is left open, that sounds restrictive. The Song presents it as the opposite: the locked garden is precious because it is kept. What is given to everyone is given to no one in particular. What is kept for one can be given to him wholly. If you have not kept the gate, the gospel does not leave you locked out. Christ cleanses and restores, and the bride he presents is made pure by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with all choicest fruits, henna with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all choice spices— a garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with all choicest fruits, henna with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all choice spices—

Behind the locked gate is not a barren patch but a paradise: pomegranates and every choice fruit, and a list of spices from across the known world, nard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh, aloes. No single garden could grow them all. The bride is every delight in one.

a garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.

And she is a source of life: a well of living water, fresh, flowing, never stagnant. A good marriage is like that for a husband: a spring that keeps refreshing him.

The phrase living water points beyond. God called himself the fountain of living waters (Jer 2:13), and Jesus promised, Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water' (John 7:38). The bride of Christ, filled with his Spirit, becomes a garden that refreshes others.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.

Now the bride speaks, and her answer is the climax of the chapter. She calls on the winds to blow through her garden and carry its fragrance to him. And then the lovely change of pronoun: my garden becomes his garden. The locked garden is opened, freely, to the one it was kept for. Let my beloved come to his garden.

This is the consummation of the marriage, told with delicacy and joy. The gate that was kept locked against everyone else is opened with gladness to her husband. Chastity was never meant to be a closed gate forever. It was keeping the garden for this.

And the pattern reaches into the Christian life. The believer's heart is a garden that belongs to Christ. When the Spirit blows on it, the spices flow, and the fruit is his: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22-23). Can you pray the bride's prayer? Let my beloved come to his garden.

4.title: You Are Altogether Beautiful, My Love
4.overview:
The bridegroom praises his bride in detail: her eyes like doves, her hair like goats flowing down Gilead, her teeth, lips, cheeks, her neck like David's tower, her breasts like twin fawns (vv. 1-5). He will stay on the mountain of myrrh until morning. You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you (vv. 6-7).

He calls her to come with him from the wild northern mountains (v. 8). She has captivated his heart with one glance; her love is better than wine, and honey and milk are under her tongue (vv. 9-11). She is a garden locked, a spring locked, a fountain sealed, full of choice fruits and every spice, a well of living water (vv. 12-15). The bride answers by opening her garden to him: Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits (v. 16).
4.theology:
Delight in a spouse's body and person is good and holy within marriage (vv. 1-7; Prov 5:18-19; Heb 13:4). Chastity before marriage and faithfulness within it keep love for one person, to be given wholly and gladly (vv. 12, 16; Prov 5:15-18; 1 Cor 7:2).

The bridegroom's no flaw in you (v. 7) anticipates Christ presenting his church without spot or blemish (Eph 5:27; Col 1:22). God is the fountain of living waters, and those who believe in Christ become sources of living water and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 15-16; John 7:38; Gal 5:22-23).
4.examples:
A flock of black goats flowing down a hillside at evening.

Specific praise instead of a generic compliment.

A garden gate kept locked, and opened gladly.

Every spice of the known world in one garden.

Praying, let my beloved come to his garden.
