verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bridegroom answers his bride's invitation: I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, and he gathers, eats and drinks of its delights; and a voice blesses the couple: Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love! (v. 1).
verseByVerse.theology: The consummation of marriage is received as a feast, and blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey, I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey, I drank my wine with my milk.

At the end of chapter 4 the bride said, Let my beloved come to his garden. Here is his answer: I came to my garden. Every line is my: my myrrh, my honeycomb, my wine. What she kept for him is now his, and he receives it with delight. The poem tells the wedding night with great restraint and great joy.

Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!

Then a voice blesses them. It may be the wedding guests, or it may be the poet himself, standing back. Whoever speaks, the message is clear: this is good. Enjoy it fully. Be drunk with love. Scripture forbids drunkenness with wine (Eph 5:18), and here it urges a husband and wife to be overcome with love for each other.

The Christian church has sometimes spoken about sex in marriage as if it were a concession. Verse 1 speaks of it as a feast, and blesses it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking (v. 2). She hesitates, having undressed and washed (v. 3). When at last she rises to open, my beloved had turned and gone (vv. 4-6). Searching the city, she is beaten by the watchmen (v. 7), and charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him I am sick with love (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Even real love can grow slow to respond, and the cost of delay is felt in the beloved's absence.

verseByVerse.quote: I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking. "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking.

A new scene, and a painful one. It is night. She is half-asleep, dozing, her heart awake. Then a sound: her husband at the door, knocking.

"Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."

He calls her by four names of love: my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one. He has been out in the night and is wet with dew. He wants to come in to her. Nothing in his words is harsh or demanding. It is an invitation, and a tender one.

The picture of a beloved knocking at the door has entered Christian devotion through the words of the risen Christ to a lukewarm church: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them? My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them?

And she hesitates. Her excuses are small: I am already undressed; I have washed my feet and would have to walk on the floor. She is comfortable. She is not refusing him. She is simply not bothered enough, just now, to get up.

Every married person knows this moment. It is not rejection or hatred. It is the slow drift of comfort, tiredness and self-concern that leaves a spouse knocking. Most marriages that cool do not end in a great quarrel. They end in a long series of doors not opened.

My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me.

He tries the latch, and at that her heart leaps. She does love him. The feeling is still there. But feeling alone has not yet got her out of bed.

The same drift happens in the life of faith. Christ calls, through his word, through a stirring in the conscience, through an opportunity to pray or serve, and we are comfortable. Our heart is moved, and we stay where we are. Jesus told his disciples to be ready to open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks (Luke 12:36). At once.

verseByVerse.quote: I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt. I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.

At last she gets up. On the bolt she finds myrrh: perhaps he had left perfume on the latch as a token of love, perhaps it was her own, put on for him. Either way, the sweetness is there on the handle, and the door opens.

I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.

And he is gone. My soul failed me when he spoke: remembering his words now pierces her. She searches and calls, and there is no answer. The moment was lost.

This is not the picture of a husband sulking. He did not break the door down, and he did not wait forever. The Song shows, simply, that delay has a cost. Opportunities for love do not stay open indefinitely.

Believers can know this too: a season when the sense of the Lord's nearness is withdrawn after we have been slow to respond. The psalmist prayed in such a season, Restore to me the joy of your salvation (Ps 51:12). The Lord does not abandon his own, but he may let us feel the absence we chose so that we learn to seek him. And the promise stands: You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart (Jer 29:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil, those watchmen of the walls. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil, those watchmen of the walls.

In chapter 3 the watchmen found her and let her pass. This time they beat her and strip her veil. Searching for him has become costly and humiliating. The Song does not explain why. It simply tells the truth that love sometimes seeks through pain, and that the people who should protect do not always do so.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love.

Bruised, she does not give up or grow bitter. She turns to the women of the city: if you find him, tell him I am sick with love. The same words she used in 2:5, when she was faint with the joy of his presence, she now uses in the pain of his absence. Her love has not changed. Only her circumstances have.

That is a mark of real love, and real faith: it longs for the beloved as much in his absence as in his presence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is your beloved more than another beloved? (v. 9). She answers: My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand (v. 10), and praises his head, eyes, cheeks, lips, arms, body and legs (vv. 11-15). His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: When asked what makes her beloved different, the bride can describe him in detail, and her delight is her testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?

The daughters of Jerusalem answer with a question, and ask it twice. What makes him so special? Why this intensity? Every woman has a beloved. What is yours more than another?

It is the question the world asks the church. You speak of Jesus as if he were more than any other teacher, any other hope, any other love. What is your beloved more than another? The bride's answer, which follows, is the model for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand. His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting beside a full pool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand.

She does not argue. She describes him. Radiant and ruddy: glowing with health and life. Distinguished among ten thousand: pick him out of any crowd. The only full description of the bridegroom in the Song is given not when he is with her, but when he is absent, and she is asked why she loves him.

His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven.

Her praise moves from his head downward, as his praise of her did in chapter 4. His head is like finest gold, precious and splendid; his hair thick and dark.

His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting beside a full pool.

He had said her eyes were doves (4:1). She says the same of his: gentle, bright, the whites clear as if bathed in milk. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in this verse is uncertain, but the picture of peace and beauty is plain.

verseByVerse.quote: His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of sweet-smelling herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh. His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels. His body is polished ivory, bedecked with sapphires. His legs are alabaster columns, set on bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of sweet-smelling herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh.

His face is fragrant; his words, from lips like lilies, are sweet as myrrh. What he says is as lovely as how he looks.

His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels. His body is polished ivory, bedecked with sapphires.

Strong arms like golden rods; a body like polished ivory. The ESV notes that one word here is uncertain and that sapphires is in Hebrew "lapis lazuli", a deep blue stone. She describes him like a precious statue, the most valuable materials in the world.

His legs are alabaster columns, set on bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.

Strong and steady as marble pillars on golden bases; tall and noble as the cedars of Lebanon. He is splendid from head to foot.

A Christian reading this cannot help asking: could I describe my Lord with half this delight? Scripture gives us far more to say than she had. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3), the image of the invisible God (Col 1:15), and the most handsome of the sons of men, with grace poured upon your lips (Ps 45:2). Many believers can explain doctrines about Christ, and few can describe him with this kind of love. The Song teaches us to try.

verseByVerse.quote: His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.

The ESV notes that mouth is in Hebrew "palate": his kisses and his words are sweetness itself. And then she sums it all up: he is altogether desirable. Just as he called her altogether beautiful (4:7), she calls him wholly, entirely desirable. There is nothing about him she would change.

This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

And her final words are the simplest and perhaps the deepest: my beloved and my friend. He is not only her lover, but her companion. The best marriages are both, passion and friendship together, and friendship is what carries a marriage through the long years when passion ebbs and flows.

Jesus offers his people the same double gift. He is the Bridegroom, and he says, I have called you friends (John 15:15). Paul, who had lost everything, said he counted it all as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). That is what it sounds like when someone finds a beloved who is altogether desirable. Can you say of him, this is my beloved, and this is my friend?

5.title: This Is My Beloved and This Is My Friend
5.overview:
The bridegroom comes to his garden and enjoys its delights, and a voice blesses the couple: Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love! (v. 1).

Then a night scene. Half-asleep, the bride hears her beloved knocking and calling tenderly, but she hesitates, comfortable and undressed (vv. 2-3). When at last she rises and opens, he has gone; she seeks and calls without answer (vv. 4-6). The watchmen beat her and take her veil (v. 7), and she charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick with love (v. 8).

They ask, What is your beloved more than another beloved? (v. 9). She describes him from head to foot: radiant, distinguished among ten thousand, his head like gold, his eyes like doves, his lips like lilies, his body like ivory, his legs like alabaster columns (vv. 10-15). He is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend (v. 16).
5.theology:
The consummation of marriage is a blessed feast (v. 1; Heb 13:4). Love must be tended; slowness to respond, even without hostility, has real costs (vv. 2-6; Luke 12:36), and those who have drifted are called to seek again with the whole heart (Jer 29:13; Ps 51:12).

Love is shown by delight in the beloved and by the ability to describe him (vv. 10-16). Christ is the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), altogether desirable to those who know him (Phil 3:8), and both Bridegroom and friend (John 15:15).
5.examples:
A marriage that cools through a long series of doors not opened.

Myrrh left on the latch.

"What is your beloved more than another?", asked of the church.

Describing someone you love to a stranger.

Beloved and friend: passion and companionship together.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?<sup>2</sup>My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.<sup>3</sup>I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.<sup>4</sup>You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.<sup>5</sup>Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.<sup>6</sup>Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young.<sup>7</sup>Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.<sup>8</sup>There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number.<sup>9</sup>My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.<sup>10</sup>"Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"<sup>11</sup>I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.<sup>12</sup>Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.<sup>13</sup>Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Where Has Your Beloved Gone?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moved by her description, the daughters of Jerusalem ask where he has gone, that we may seek him with you (v. 1). She knows: My beloved has gone down to his garden (v. 2). I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride's delight in her beloved makes others want to seek him, and in his absence she rests in belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?

A remarkable change. In 5:9 the daughters of Jerusalem asked, with some doubt, what made her beloved special. She answered by describing him with love (5:10-16). Now they are not asking why; they are asking where. That we may seek him with you. Her description has made them want him too.

That is how people are drawn to Christ. Not usually by argument first, but by hearing someone who loves him describe him. When believers speak of their Lord with delight, others begin to ask where he may be found. If no one has ever asked you where to seek him, ask yourself how often they have heard you describe him.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.

She knows where he is. In chapter 5 she searched the city in vain. Now she answers without hesitation: in his garden. And in the Song the garden is his bride herself (4:12, 16; 5:1). He has not gone far after all. He has gone where he belongs, to her.

The ESV notes that to graze may be rendered "to pasture his flock", here and in verse 3. The shepherd is among his lilies.

I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.

The words of 2:16 return, but reversed. There she said, My beloved is mine, and I am his. Now, after the night of loss, she begins with his claim on her: I am my beloved's. When she felt most unsure of her grip on him, she rested in his grip on her.

That is the comfort of the believer in a season of spiritual dryness. Feelings of nearness come and go. The covenant does not. I am my beloved's. Jesus said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — My Dove, My Perfect One, Is the Only One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He greets her as before: You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, her eyes overwhelming him, and he repeats his earlier praise word for word (vv. 4-7). Among sixty queens and eighty concubines, My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, and even the queens praise her (vv. 8-9): Who is this who looks down like the dawn? (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Love restored speaks the same words it spoke before, and to the husband his wife is the only one.

verseByVerse.quote: You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.

He speaks, and his first words are praise. After the scene of the closed door, the reader might expect reproach. There is none. She is beautiful as Tirzah, a city famous for its beauty and for a time a royal capital of the northern kingdom, and lovely as Jerusalem, the city of God.

And awesome as an army with banners: her beauty is not only gentle but majestic, overwhelming, like a great army marching with its standards raised. A husband who loves his wife is not only charmed by her. He is in awe of her.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.

Her eyes overwhelm him; he can hardly bear to look into them. The mighty king is undone by one look from his bride, as he was in 4:9.

Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.

Now notice: these lines are almost exactly the words he spoke in 4:1-3, before the door was left closed. He does not compose new, cooler praise. He says the same thing he said before. Her hesitation has not changed how he sees her.

That is what forgiveness looks like in a marriage. Not "I will love you again when you have earned it", but the same words, the same delight, restored. And it is how Christ restores his people. After Peter denied him, the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61-62). But the risen Lord did not give Peter a lesser place. He gave him back his calling.

verseByVerse.quote: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number. My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number.

A king's palace was full of women: queens, concubines, young women beyond counting. He could have anyone.

My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.

And yet: the only one. He says it twice. Among all the women he could have, she is the one. That is the shape of love as God designed it: one man, one woman, each the only one to the other. They shall become one flesh. The Song lifts up this ideal even though the kings of Israel, Solomon among them, so often fell short of it.

And the other women do not resent her. They called her blessed, and they praised her. Her beauty and his love are so evident that even rivals admire. So the church, loved by Christ as his only bride, is meant to be a people whom even the world cannot help admiring.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"

These seem to be the words of the queens and the young women. They see her and reach for the largest pictures they have: the dawn breaking, the moon, the sun, a marching army. She rises like morning light and shines like the heavens.

The woman of chapter 1 said, Do not gaze at me because I am dark (1:6). Now she is described as bright as the sun. That is what love has done for her. A bride who is truly loved begins to shine. And the church, loved by Christ, will one day shine as he does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She went down to the nut orchard to see the spring blossoms (v. 11), and Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince (v. 12). The others call, Return, return, O Shulammite, that they may look on her (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride is named, called back and admired; love's joy draws others to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom. Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.

She went down to see the spring: blossoms, vine buds, pomegranate flowers. Spring in the Song is the season of love (2:11-13), and the garden is the place of love.

Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.

This is one of the hardest verses in the Song to understand, and it should be held lightly. The ESV notes that the last phrase may be rendered "chariots of Ammi-Nadib", which could be a name. The general sense seems to be that, before she knew it, her desire carried her away into a place of honour, as if swept up into a royal chariot beside her prince. Love surprised her and lifted her up.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?

The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 7. For the first and only time the bride has a name, or a title: the Shulammite. The others call her back four times, Return, return, because they want to see her.

And someone answers, perhaps the bride herself, perhaps the bridegroom: why do you gaze on her as upon a dance before two armies? The ESV notes that this may be rendered "dance of Mahanaim". It seems to picture a festive dance that draws every eye. The next chapter begins the bridegroom's own praise of her as she dances.

The woman who did not want to be looked at in chapter 1 is now the one everyone wants to see. Love has done that. And the chorus Return, return is a lovely call for anyone who has wandered: come back, so that we may see you again among us.

6.title: I Am My Beloved's and My Beloved Is Mine
6.overview:
Moved by the bride's description, the daughters of Jerusalem ask where her beloved has gone, so that they may seek him with her (v. 1). She knows: he has gone down to his garden. I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (vv. 2-3).

The bridegroom greets her without reproach: beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners; her eyes overwhelm him, and he repeats his earlier praise word for word (vv. 4-7). Among sixty queens and eighty concubines, she is the only one, and the queens themselves praise her, asking who this is who looks down like the dawn (vv. 8-10).

She went down to see the spring blossoms, and before she knew it her desire carried her among the chariots of a prince (vv. 11-12). The others call, Return, return, O Shulammite, that they may look upon her (v. 13).
6.theology:
Delight in the beloved draws others to seek him (v. 1); the church's love for Christ is part of its witness. In seasons of absence, the believer rests in belonging to the Lord (v. 3; John 6:37).

Love restored speaks the same words as before; forgiveness does not demote the forgiven (vv. 5-7; Luke 22:61-62). God's design for marriage is one man and one woman, each the only one to the other (vv. 8-9; Gen 2:24). The loved bride shines (v. 10), as Christ's church will.
6.examples:
Being asked where to find someone you have described with love.

Resting in "I am his" when "he is mine" feels uncertain.

The same words of praise after a quarrel.

Sixty queens, and one wife who is the only one.

The woman who hid her face, now bright as the sun.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand.<sup>2</sup>Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.<sup>3</sup>Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.<sup>4</sup>Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.<sup>5</sup>Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.<sup>6</sup>How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights!<sup>7</sup>Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.<sup>8</sup>I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples,<sup>9</sup>and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.<sup>10</sup>I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.<sup>11</sup>Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages;<sup>12</sup>let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.<sup>13</sup>The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — How Beautiful and Pleasant You Are
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bridegroom praises his bride from her feet upward: her sandalled feet and rounded thighs (vv. 1-2), her breasts like fawns, her neck like an ivory tower, her eyes like pools, her head crowned like Carmel, so that a king is held captive in the tresses (vv. 3-5). How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! (v. 6). He climbs the palm tree to take its fruit, and her mouth is like the best wine (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Delight in one's own spouse, spoken openly and specifically, is a gift of God and a duty of love.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand. Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand.

In chapter 4 the bridegroom praised his bride from her eyes downward. Here he begins at her feet and works upward. The setting seems to be the dance of 6:13; he watches her move and speaks what he sees.

He calls her O noble daughter, a king's word of honour, and says her thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand. That is a quiet act of worship. Her body is craftsmanship, and someone made it. The psalmist says the same of himself: I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made (Ps 139:14).

Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.

A bowl of wine and a heap of wheat: the two staples of a feast, drink and bread. She is nourishment and celebration to him. The images are agricultural because the Song comes from a farming world, and they are meant warmly: abundance, plenty, harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.

He repeats the picture of 4:5, and adds new ones. Her neck is an ivory tower, pale and stately. Her eyes are deep, still pools at the city gate, where people gathered and lingered. Her nose is like a watchtower looking north: strong, well set, noble. To modern ears that is a strange compliment; in a world that prized a straight, strong profile it was high praise.

Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.

Mount Carmel rises green above the sea, and her head is carried like that. Her hair is dark as royal purple, and in it the king is a prisoner. He has an army, a throne and a palace, and he is captured by his wife's hair. That is how he wants it.

Husbands, notice again the sheer specificity. He does not say she looks nice. He names her feet, her neck, her eyes, her hair. Detail is the proof of attention, and attention is the shape love takes when it is awake.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights!

He sums it up. The ESV notes that with all your delights may be rendered "among delights". She is beautiful and she is pleasant: lovely to look at and lovely to be with. Beauty without pleasantness soon wears thin, and pleasantness makes beauty last. He has both in her, and he says so.

Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.

Tall and graceful as a date palm, heavy with fruit. The palm was a tree of the oasis: shade, sweetness and life in a dry land.

verseByVerse.quote: I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples, and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples,

Having compared her to a palm, he says he will climb it. The Song does not pretend that desire is polite. It is frank, and it is directed entirely to his own wife. That is the point. The same Bible that says everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28) gives a husband these words for his own bride.

and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.

The ESV notes that mouth is in Hebrew "palate", and that the last clause is difficult: the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate read as the ESV does, while the Hebrew reads "causing the lips of sleepers to speak", or "gliding over the lips of those who sleep". Her kiss is like the best wine, and it is his.

Notice who is speaking in the last words: for my beloved. In the middle of his praise she answers, taking his words into her own mouth. They are no longer two voices taking turns. They finish each other's lines.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — Come, My Beloved, Let Us Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (v. 10). She invites him out to the fields and villages, to the vineyards to see whether the vines have budded: There I will give you my love (vv. 11-12). The mandrakes give fragrance, and beside their doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Mature love rests in being desired and takes the initiative in giving itself.

verseByVerse.quote: I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.

Here is the refrain for the third and last time, and it has changed again. In 2:16 she said, My beloved is mine, and I am his. In 6:3, after the night she lost him, she began with belonging: I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine. Now she says only the second half, and adds something new: his desire is for me.

That is where love arrives when it matures. Not "he is mine", asserting a claim. Not even "I am his", stating a duty. But resting in the settled knowledge that he wants her. A wife who knows her husband desires her, and a husband who knows his wife delights in him, can weather a great deal.

And it is where the soul arrives with God. The believer's peace is not finally in the strength of his grip on Christ, but in knowing that Christ desires him. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa 62:5). Can you say it: his desire is for me?

verseByVerse.quote: Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages; let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages;

Now she takes the initiative. In chapter 2 he came to her window and said, Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away. Now she says it to him: Come, my beloved, let us go out. The ESV notes that in the villages may be rendered "among the henna plants". Either way, she wants to get away with him.

let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.

She plans it: out early, to the vineyards, to see the spring. And There I will give you my love. Desire in marriage is not only the husband's to express. Paul says as much: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband (1 Cor 7:3).

There is practical wisdom here too. Love needs occasions made for it. They go out early, away from the house and the work, to a place they both love. Marriages are kept alive by such plans.

verseByVerse.quote: The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.

Mandrakes were associated with love and fertility in the ancient world; Rachel and Leah once quarrelled over them (Gen 30:14). Their scent fills the air, and at their own doors there is fruit of every kind.

Then the loveliest phrase: new as well as old, which I have laid up for you. She has been storing up delights for him: some fresh, some kept from earlier seasons. A marriage that lasts has both. New joys, and the treasured old ones: the remembered honeymoon, the family jokes, the hard years survived together. Nothing is wasted; everything is laid up for the beloved.

What have you laid up for your husband or wife, and when did you last bring it out? And what have you laid up for the Lord, who receives every act of love done in his name, new and old alike?

7.title: His Desire Is for Me
7.overview:
The bridegroom praises his bride from her feet upward as she dances: her sandalled feet, her thighs like jewels, her body like a bowl of wine and a heap of wheat (vv. 1-2), her breasts like fawns, her neck an ivory tower, her eyes pools in Heshbon, her head crowned like Carmel, her hair holding a king captive (vv. 3-5). How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! (v. 6). He will climb the palm tree and take its fruit, and her mouth is like the best wine (vv. 7-9).

I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (v. 10). She invites him out early to the fields and vineyards to see the spring, and there she will give him her love (vv. 11-12). At their own doors are choice fruits, new and old, which she has laid up for him (v. 13).
7.theology:
The body is God's craftsmanship, and delight in one's own spouse is holy (vv. 1-9; Ps 139:14; Heb 13:4). Such desire is directed to one's spouse alone, in contrast to lust (Matt 5:28).

Mature love rests in being desired (v. 10), as faith rests in Christ's love for us rather than in the strength of our love for him (1 John 4:19; Isa 62:5). Love is mutual in its initiative and its giving (vv. 11-13; 1 Cor 7:3-4).
7.examples:
A king held captive by his wife's hair.

Naming her feet, her neck, her eyes: detail as the proof of attention.

Finishing each other's sentences.

Going out early, away from the house and the work.

Delights laid up and kept, new and old.

If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me.<sup>2</sup>I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Oh That You Were Like a Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She wishes she could show her love openly without shame, and bring him into her mother's house (vv. 1-2). His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! (v. 3). And for the third time: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Love longs to be public as well as private, and still guards its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you were like a brother to me who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me. I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that you were like a brother to me who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me.

In her world a woman could kiss a brother in the street and no one would think anything of it; to kiss a husband in public would be scandalous. So she wishes, oddly and touchingly, that he were her brother, not instead of her husband, but so that her love could be shown anywhere without a raised eyebrow.

Love wants to be open. Something is wrong when a marriage is affectionate behind closed doors and cold in company. She would like the whole street to see.

I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate.

She would bring him home, to the house where she was taught, and give him her best: spiced wine, pomegranate juice. Love gives what it has, and gives it in the place where it was raised.

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!

The words of 2:6 return, unchanged. Whatever has happened in between, the closed door and the night search and the beating by the watchmen, the embrace is the same. That is a testimony in a single line: after everything, here they still are.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.

And the refrain for the third time (2:7; 3:5). It is the most repeated sentence in the book. A book this frank about desire says three times: do not awaken it before its time. Those two things are not in tension. Only what is precious needs guarding.

The Song is about to tell us how strong this love is. Precisely because it is that strong, it must not be played with.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? (v. 5). Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave, the very flame of the LORD (v. 6). Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it, and no wealth can buy it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The Song's climax: love that death cannot break, floods cannot drown and money cannot buy, because its flame is from the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?

A question from onlookers, echoing 3:6, where a royal procession came up from the wilderness in clouds of perfume. This time it is not a litter carried by soldiers. It is a woman walking, leaning on her beloved. The grandeur has become intimacy. Two people coming home from the wilderness, and she is leaning on him.

That image has comforted Christians for centuries, and rightly, because the pilgrim's journey through the wilderness of this world is made leaning on Christ. But notice that the Song's picture is already tender at the human level: the strength a husband and wife become to each other over years.

Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.

The speaker is hard to identify, and the lines are mysterious. Under the apple tree, where love was awakened, is the very place where his mother gave birth to him. Life and love belong to the same ground. Marriage is where new life comes from, and it is a reminder that every beloved was once someone's newborn child.

verseByVerse.quote: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,

Here is the summit of the Song. A seal was a signet, a ring or cylinder that carried a person's name and stamped his documents; to wear one was to carry an identity. Set me as a seal upon your heart: let me be what you carry closest, what marks who you are, on the inside, where love is felt, and on the arm, where it is seen and where it works. Israel was told to bind God's words on the hand (Deut 6:8), and the high priest carried the names of the tribes on his heart when he went in before God (Exod 28:29).

for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave.

Why does she ask it? Because love is that serious. Strong as death. Nothing in human experience is as irresistible as death; it takes everyone, and no one refuses it. Love is like that, the poem says: it lays hold of a person and will not let go. And jealousy is fierce as the grave: the ESV notes that jealousy may be rendered "ardor", and that the grave is in Hebrew "as Sheol". This is not petty suspicion. It is the rightful passion of love that will not share the beloved. Love by its nature is exclusive.

Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.

And here, once only in the whole book, God is named. Love's flame is the very flame of the LORD. That single phrase tells us where this fire comes from. Human love is not merely a chemical accident or a social arrangement. It burns with a flame kindled from the love of God himself. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

And it is in this verse that the Song reaches farthest toward Christ, whose love was in fact strong as death, and stronger. He went into death for his bride and came back. He carries his people as a seal: Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (Isa 49:16). And he has sealed them to himself: believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Eph 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it.

Fire is put out by water; this fire is not. Pour the sea on it and it burns. That is a promise to hold in the hard years. Floods do come to a marriage: illness, poverty, grief, betrayal, the slow wearing of time. Real love is not extinguished by them. Many marriages end not because the floods were too strong but because the fire was never the flame of the LORD.

And for the believer this is the settled ground of everything. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you (Isa 43:2). Nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:39). Having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1).

If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.

Love cannot be bought. A man who tried to purchase it with everything he owned would be laughed at, and rightly: he would have shown that he did not know what love is. It is not a commodity. It can only be given and received.

Which is why the gospel is not a transaction. No one buys God's love; it is given. And the only right response is the response of the merchant who found one pearl of great value and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46): not paying for love, but letting go of everything else for the sake of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Vineyard and the Final Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The brothers ask what to do for their little sister when she is spoken for; they will build or enclose her (vv. 8-9). I was a wall, she answers, and she found peace in his eyes (v. 10). Solomon may keep the thousand pieces of silver from his vineyard; My vineyard, my very own, is before me (vv. 11-12). He asks to hear her voice, and she calls, Make haste, my beloved (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Purity kept, love owned and not sold, and a last call for the beloved to come.

verseByVerse.quote: We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for? If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver, but if she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for?

Other voices now: her brothers, probably the same brothers who made her work the vineyards in 1:6. They are looking at a younger sister, still a child, and asking what to do for her when a suitor comes.

If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver, but if she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.

Two pictures. If she proves to be a wall, keeping herself, they will honour her, crowning the wall with silver. If she proves to be a door, open to anyone, they will board her up. Their concern is her purity, and their instinct is protection.

Parents and brothers and churches still face this question: what shall we do for the young, before the day comes when they are spoken for? The Song's answer is neither neglect nor imprisonment, but preparation and honour. And the aim is not merely to prevent something; it is to keep something for its time, so that it can be given whole. For this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3).

verseByVerse.quote: I was a wall, and my breasts were like towers; then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was a wall, and my breasts were like towers; then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.

She answers for herself: I was a wall. She kept herself. She is grown now, and she has not been a door open to everyone. And the result: then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace. The ESV notes that finds may be rendered "brings out": she found peace, or she brought peace to him. Both are true of a faithful wife.

Notice what she did not say. She did not say, I was a wall, so I missed out. The woman who kept the gate locked is the woman of chapters 4 to 7, who knows love at its richest. Purity is not the enemy of passion. It is its protection.

For those who cannot say I was a wall, the gospel has a word. Christ makes the unclean clean, and presents his bride without blemish (Eph 5:27). No past puts a person beyond that mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; each one was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; each one was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver.

A vineyard let out to tenants for a thousand pieces of silver: a business arrangement, love as an estate managed for profit. Solomon, the king with a palace full of women, had vineyards of that kind.

My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.

And here the bride speaks with quiet magnificence. Keep your thousand, Solomon. Pay your keepers. My vineyard, my very own, is before me. She has one vineyard, her own love and her own husband, and she would not trade it for a royal estate.

Remember how she began: they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept! (1:6). The book that opened with a woman who had no vineyard of her own ends with her holding it, and it is worth more to her than everything Solomon owns. That is the Song's verdict on love: one faithful marriage is richer than a kingdom of arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: O you who dwell in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice; let me hear it. Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O you who dwell in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice; let me hear it.

Almost the last words of the bridegroom, and they are a request to hear her voice. He asked the same in 2:14: let me hear your voice. Of everything he could ask for at the end of the Song, he asks for her speech. Love never gets tired of the beloved's voice.

Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.

And the bride has the last word, as she had the first (1:2). It is not a conclusion but a call: Make haste, my beloved. Come quickly. Be like a young stag over the fragrant hills. The Song ends in longing, with the lovers still reaching for each other. That is honest. This side of eternity love is never finished; it always wants more.

And the Bible ends the same way. The Spirit and the Bride say to the Bridegroom, Come (Rev 22:17), and he answers, Surely I am coming soon, and the church replies, Come, Lord Jesus! (Rev 22:20). The last prayer of the Song of Songs and the last prayer of Scripture are the same prayer. Whoever has learned to say Make haste, my beloved to a husband or a wife has learned something of what it means to wait for Christ; and whoever has learned to say it to Christ has found the love that is strong as death, and stronger.

8.title: Love Is Strong as Death
8.overview:
The bride wishes her love could be shown openly, and would bring her beloved into her mother's house (vv. 1-2). His embrace is as it was (v. 3), and for the third time she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time (v. 4).

Someone asks who is coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved (v. 5). Then the Song's summit: Set me as a seal upon your heart, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD (v. 6). Many waters cannot quench love, and a man who offered all his wealth for it would be despised (v. 7).

Her brothers plan how to protect their little sister (vv. 8-9); she answers, I was a wall, and found peace in his eyes (v. 10). Solomon may keep the thousand pieces of silver from his rented vineyard: her own vineyard is her own (vv. 11-12). He asks to hear her voice, and she calls, Make haste, my beloved (vv. 13-14).
8.theology:
Love is to be guarded until its time (v. 4), and it must be guarded because it is strong as death and exclusive by nature (v. 6). Its flame is kindled by God himself, the one mention of the LORD in the book (v. 6; 1 John 4:19).

Love cannot be drowned or bought (v. 7): Christ's love for his people cannot be separated from them (Rom 8:39; John 13:1), and it is given, never purchased (Matt 13:46). Purity kept is honoured and brings peace (vv. 9-10; 1 Thess 4:3), and where it was not kept, Christ still presents his bride without blemish (Eph 5:27).

The Song ends in longing for the beloved to come, as Scripture ends with the Bride calling the Bridegroom (vv. 13-14; Rev 22:17, 20).
8.examples:
Affection behind closed doors and coldness in company.

Two people walking home from the wilderness, one leaning on the other.

A signet worn where it is felt and where it is seen.

Pouring the sea on a fire that will not go out.

A man trying to buy love with everything he owns.

Keep your thousand, Solomon: my vineyard is my own.
